subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: The electric potential at point P, produced by nearby fixed charged objects, is +50 V. Which statement correctly interprets this value?
options: A particle of charge q placed at P adds U_E = q(50 V) to the system.
Any charged particle placed at P has 50 J of electric potential energy.
The electric field produced at P by the objects is 50 V/m.
P has no electric potential until a charge is placed there.
optionWhy: Potential is electric potential energy per unit charge. With a charge q at P, the system's electric potential energy is U_E = qV = q(50 V), which is 50 J for every coulomb of charge placed there.
A student who treats the potential as the energy of whatever is placed at P picks this. 50 V means 50 J per coulomb: a particle of charge q gives U_E = q(50 V), which depends on q.
A student who takes the potential's value as the field's magnitude picks this. The field depends on how the potential changes near P, |ΔV/Δr|, which the value 50 V at one point does not give.
A student who thinks a potential needs a charge at the point picks this. The fixed charged objects produce the potential at P whether or not anything is there; a charge placed at P only reveals it.
questions.explain: Potential is electric potential energy per unit charge. With a charge q at P, the system's electric potential energy is U_E = qV = q(50 V), which is 50 J for every coulomb of charge placed there.
questions.working: V = U_E/q, so U_E = qV = q(+50 V) = (50 J/C)q.

questions.q: Which statement best describes how a battery maintains a potential difference between its terminals?
options: Chemical reactions make new charge, which then collects at the two terminals.
A store of charge put in when it was made keeps its terminals charged until used up.
It pushes out a fixed current, and the potential difference follows from that current.
Chemical reactions move positive and negative charge apart, to opposite terminals.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a battery produces charge picks this. Charge is conserved: the reactions separate existing charge; they do not create it.
A student who pictures a battery as a container of charge picks this. The battery keeps separating charge chemically; what runs down is the chemical energy available, not a supply of charge.
A student who treats a battery as a constant-current source picks this. A battery maintains a potential difference; the current it delivers depends on what is connected to it.

The chemical processes in the battery separate charge that is already present, building up positive charge at one terminal and negative charge at the other. That separation of charge is what produces the potential difference.
questions.explain: The chemical processes in the battery separate charge that is already present, building up positive charge at one terminal and negative charge at the other. That separation of charge is what produces the potential difference.

questions.q: Two metal spheres of different radii are far apart. One is charged and the other is uncharged. They are then connected by a long thin conducting wire. After the charges stop moving, which quantity is the same for the two spheres?
options: The electric potential at the surface of each sphere
The amount of excess charge on each of the two spheres
The excess charge per unit area of each sphere's surface
The magnitude of the electric field just outside each sphere
optionWhy: Electrons move through the wire as long as there is a potential difference between the spheres. They stop when the surfaces are at the same potential, which is the equilibrium condition for conductors in contact.

A student who thinks connected conductors share charge equally picks this. Charge moves until the potentials are equal; spheres of different radii then carry different charges, the larger sphere the larger charge.

A student who thinks the charge spreads evenly over the combined surface picks this. Equal potentials, not equal charge per unit area, set the final state; the smaller sphere ends with the greater charge per unit area.

A student who expects charge flow to stop when the fields balance picks this. Charge moves between the spheres while there is a potential difference between them, so the potentials become equal; the fields outside the two spheres differ.
questions.explain: Electrons move through the wire as long as there is a potential difference between the spheres. They stop when the surfaces are at the same potential, which is the equilibrium condition for conductors in contact.

questions.q: A battery is connected to a lightbulb by copper wires. Which statement best explains why charge moves through the wires?
options: The battery releases stored charge into wires that had no free charge.
The battery's emf is a force, in newtons, that pushes on each charge directly.
The battery's potential difference makes charges already in the wires move.
Charge flows out of both battery terminals and meets in the bulb filament.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a battery is a store of charge picks this. The wires contain vast numbers of free electrons before the battery is connected; the battery's potential difference sets them moving, and the same charge circulates around the circuit.

A student who takes the name 'electromotive force' literally picks this. An emf is a potential difference, measured in volts; the forces on the charges come from the electric field that this potential difference sets up in the circuit.

The wires and filament are full of free electrons before the battery is connected. The battery provides a potential difference (its emf), which sets up an electric field in the circuit, and the charges already present move in response. The battery does not supply the charge.

A student who pictures charge leaving both terminals picks this. Charge moves around the loop in one direction: conventional current leaves the positive terminal and returns to the negative terminal, and electrons move the opposite way.
questions.explain: The wires and filament are full of free electrons before the battery is connected. The battery provides a potential difference (its emf), which sets up an electric field in the circuit, and the charges already present move in response. The battery does not supply the charge.

questions.q: A length of copper wire is not connected to anything, so there is no current in it. Which statement correctly describes the free electrons in the wire?
options: They are at rest, because a current is needed to set the carriers moving.
There are none; free electrons enter a wire from a battery connected to it.
They are fixed in place; in a metal, the positive charges are what move.
They move in random directions, so their net motion through the wire is zero.
optionWhy: A student who thinks no current means no moving charge picks this. The free electrons are moving, rapidly and randomly; there is no current because their motion has no net direction.

A student who thinks the charge in a circuit comes from the battery picks this. Copper contains an enormous number of free electrons whether or not it is connected to anything; a battery sets them drifting in one direction.
A student who thinks positive charges carry the current in metals picks this. In a metal the positive ions are held in place; the free electrons are the charges that move.

Zero current means zero net motion of the charge carriers, not zero motion. The free electrons in the copper move rapidly in random directions, so as many cross any cross-section one way as the other, and no net charge is carried along the wire.
questions.explain: Zero current means zero net motion of the charge carriers, not zero motion. The free electrons in the copper move rapidly in random directions, so as many cross any cross-section one way as the other, and no net charge is carried along the wire.

questions.q: The diagram shows positive and negative ions moving through a solution between ends X and Y. The labels give the magnitude of the charge that each kind of ion carries through the cross-section shown each second. What is the current through the cross-section?
options: 3.0 A toward Y
1.0 A toward Y
5.0 A toward X
2.0 A toward X
optionWhy: A student who takes the current to be in the direction the negative carriers move, and counts only them, picks this. Conventional current is the direction positive charge would move: the negative ions moving toward Y make a current toward X, and the positive ions add to it.

A student who thinks flows in opposite directions cancel picks this: 3.0 − 2.0 = 1.0. Negative charge moving toward Y and positive charge moving toward X both make conventional current toward X, so they add.

Conventional current is in the direction positive charge moves. The positive ions carry 2.0 C each second toward X: 2.0 A toward X. The negative ions carry 3.0 C each second toward Y, which is equivalent to positive charge moving toward X: 3.0 A toward X. Both contributions point the same way, so the current is 5.0 A toward X.

A student who thinks only positive charges count toward conventional current picks this. The negative ions carry charge too; their motion toward Y is a current of 3.0 A toward X, which adds to the 2.0 A.
questions.explain: Conventional current is in the direction positive charge moves. The positive ions carry 2.0 C each second toward X: 2.0 A toward X. The negative ions carry 3.0 C each second toward Y, which is equivalent to positive charge moving toward X: 3.0 A toward X. Both contributions point the same way, so the current is 5.0 A toward X.
questions.working: Positive ions: 2.0 C/s toward X, a current of 2.0 A toward X. Negative ions: 3.0 C/s of negative charge toward Y, a current of 3.0 A toward X. Total I = 2.0 A + 3.0 A = 5.0 A toward X.

questions.q: A flashlight contains a battery, a switch and a bulb, connected by metal strips into a single loop. With the switch closed, the bulb lights. Which statement correctly describes the charges that move through the bulb?
options: They are charges stored in the battery that flow out to the bulb and are used up there.
They flow out of both terminals of the battery and meet inside the bulb's filament.
They are charges already present throughout the loop, set moving around it by the battery.
They reach the bulb through one strip, while the other strip carries no charge.
optionWhy: A student who pictures the battery as a store of charge picks this. The battery does not hold a supply of charge for the bulb to consume: charge is conserved and circulates around the loop, and what the bulb transfers is energy.

A student who thinks charge comes out of both battery terminals picks this. Charge moves one way around the loop: in conventional current, out of the positive terminal, through the bulb, and back into the negative terminal.

A circuit is a loop, and charges are present in every part of it: the strips, the bulb and the battery itself. The battery makes them move around the loop, so the same charges pass through the bulb, return to the battery and pass through it. The bulb transfers energy; it does not use up charge.

A student who thinks one strip delivers the charge and the other is idle picks this. Charge flows only around a complete loop: one strip leads it to the bulb and the other leads it back to the battery, with the same current in both.
questions.explain: A circuit is a loop, and charges are present in every part of it: the strips, the bulb and the battery itself. The battery makes them move around the loop, so the same charges pass through the bulb, return to the battery and pass through it. The bulb transfers energy; it does not use up charge.

questions.q: Which description states what a circuit schematic represents?
options: Where each element sits in the real circuit, drawn roughly to scale
The order in which charge reaches the elements, which sets their effect
Which elements are joined to which, whatever their real positions
The route of the electrons, drawn from the battery's negative terminal
optionWhy: A student who reads a schematic as a scale drawing picks this. Positions and wire lengths on a schematic carry no meaning; only the connections do.

A student who thinks charge meets the elements in turn picks this. A gap or change anywhere in a loop affects every element in that loop, so the order of the elements around a loop does not matter; a schematic records connections, not an order.

A schematic records connections: which points each element's two terminals are joined to. Moving an element on the page, or drawing a wire longer or bent, gives the same circuit as long as the connections are unchanged.

A student who thinks schematics show the motion of electrons picks this. Unless otherwise specified, schematics use conventional current, from the positive terminal around to the negative; and what a schematic records is connections, not a route.
questions.explain: A schematic records connections: which points each element's two terminals are joined to. Moving an element on the page, or drawing a wire longer or bent, gives the same circuit as long as the connections are unchanged.

questions.q: The circuit shown contains an element labeled E. What does the symbol for E represent?
options: A battery giving an adjustable potential difference
A capacitor whose capacitance can be adjusted
A capacitor that is disconnected from the loop
A capacitor with the current directed along the arrow
optionWhy: A student who reads any pair of parallel plates as a battery picks this. A battery, like the one on the left of the circuit, has one long thin plate and one short thick plate; E's two plates are equal, the symbol for a capacitor.
Two equal parallel plates are the symbol for a capacitor, and a diagonal arrow drawn across a standard symbol marks a variable element. E is therefore a variable capacitor.
A student who reads the line across the symbol as crossing it out picks this. A diagonal arrow across a symbol means the element is variable; E is still connected in the loop.
A student who reads every arrow on a schematic as a current direction picks this. The diagonal arrow marks E as adjustable; it says nothing about the direction of any current.
questions.explain: Two equal parallel plates are the symbol for a capacitor, and a diagonal arrow drawn across a standard symbol marks a variable element. E is therefore a variable capacitor.

questions.q: Resistor P has a greater resistance than resistor Q. Which statement correctly describes what this means?
options: P uses up a larger share of the current that flows into it than Q does.
With equal ΔV across each, less charge passes through P per second.
P is made of a material that conducts charge less well than Q's material.
P has the larger potential difference across it in every circuit.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a resistor uses up current picks this. The current leaving any resistor equals the current entering it; a larger resistance limits the current for a given ΔV, it does not consume any of it.

Resistance measures how strongly an object opposes the movement of charge. With the same potential difference across each resistor, the one that opposes the movement more, P, has less charge passing through it each second: a smaller current, I = ΔV/R.
A student who thinks resistance depends only on the material picks this. P and Q could be made of the same material: P could simply be longer or thinner. Resistance belongs to the object, R = ρℓ/A.

A student who reads R = ΔV/I as R ∝ ΔV picks this. The potential difference across a resistor depends on the circuit it is in; a larger resistance does not mean a larger ΔV in every circuit, for example when P and Q are connected to different batteries.
questions.explain: Resistance measures how strongly an object opposes the movement of charge. With the same potential difference across each resistor, the one that opposes the movement more, P, has less charge passing through it each second: a smaller current, I = ΔV/R.

questions.q: The current in a resistor is increased, and the resistor warms up. Which property must the resistor's material have for the resistor to remain ohmic?
options: Its resistivity is small, as it is for a good conductor.
Its resistance increases in proportion to the applied ΔV.
Its dimensions stay fixed as its temperature changes.
Its resistivity stays the same as its temperature changes.
optionWhy: A student who links 'ohmic' with good conductors picks this. Being ohmic concerns whether the resistivity stays constant, not how small it is; tungsten is a good conductor, but a tungsten filament is not ohmic over its working range.
A student who reads R = ΔV/I as R ∝ ΔV picks this. An ohmic material has the opposite property: its resistance stays constant when ΔV changes.

A student who thinks temperature affects resistance only through the size of a resistor picks this. Temperature changes resistance mainly by changing the resistivity; the ohmic model requires the resistivity to stay constant.
An ohmic material has a constant resistance for all currents, and its resistivity is constant regardless of temperature. So even as a resistor made from it warms up, its resistance does not change.
questions.explain: An ohmic material has a constant resistance for all currents, and its resistivity is constant regardless of temperature. So even as a resistor made from it warms up, its resistance does not change.

questions.q: A length ℓ of wire with diameter d is made of a material of resistivity ρ. The wire is connected to an ideal battery so that the potential difference across it is ΔV. Which expression gives the current I in the wire?
options: I = πd²ΔV/(4ρℓ)
I = 4ρℓΔV/(πd²)
I = 4ΔV/(πd²ρℓ)
I = πd²ΔV/(2ρℓ)
optionWhy: The cross-sectional area is A = π(d/2)² = πd²/4, so R = ρℓ/A = 4ρℓ/(πd²). Ohm's law then gives I = ΔV/R = πd²ΔV/(4ρℓ).
A student who multiplies ΔV by R instead of dividing picks this. Ohm's law is I = ΔV/R: a larger resistance gives a smaller current, so R belongs in the denominator. (Units check: V·Ω is not A.)
A student who thinks a thicker wire has more resistance, R = ρℓA, picks this. Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, R = ρℓ/A, so the area belongs in the numerator of I.
A student who squares only the numerator of d/2, writing A = πd²/2, picks this. (d/2)² = d²/4, so A = πd²/4 and the current is half this value.
questions.explain: The cross-sectional area is A = π(d/2)² = πd²/4, so R = ρℓ/A = 4ρℓ/(πd²). Ohm's law then gives I = ΔV/R = πd²ΔV/(4ρℓ).
questions.working: A = π(d/2)² = πd²/4. R = ρℓ/A = 4ρℓ/(πd²). I = ΔV/R = πd²ΔV/(4ρℓ). (Errors: I = ΔV·R gives 4ρℓΔV/(πd²); R = ρℓA gives I = ΔV/(ρℓ·πd²/4) = 4ΔV/(πd²ρℓ); A = πd²/2 gives πd²ΔV/(2ρℓ).)

questions.q: Resistors of 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω are connected in parallel. Without calculating, which statement correctly describes their equivalent resistance R_eq?
options: R_eq is between 10 Ω and 30 Ω.
R_eq is smaller than 10 Ω.
R_eq is larger than 30 Ω.
R_eq equals the smallest, 10 Ω.
optionWhy: A student who treats the equivalent resistance as a kind of average picks this. Adding paths in parallel lowers the resistance below that of any single path, so R_eq is less than the smallest resistance, 10 Ω.

Each resistor connected in parallel gives charge another path, so the equivalent resistance decreases as paths are added. Even the 10 Ω resistor alone would have a resistance of 10 Ω; with two more paths, R_eq is less than that (it is 5.5 Ω).
A student who thinks adding any resistor increases the total resistance picks this. That is true for resistors in series; resistors in parallel add paths for charge, so R_eq is less than 10 Ω.

A student who thinks all the current takes the path of least resistance picks this, treating the group as the 10 Ω resistor alone. The 20 Ω and 30 Ω paths also carry current, so R_eq is less than 10 Ω.
questions.explain: Each resistor connected in parallel gives charge another path, so the equivalent resistance decreases as paths are added. Even the 10 Ω resistor alone would have a resistance of 10 Ω; with two more paths, R_eq is less than that (it is 5.5 Ω).
questions.working: Each path added in parallel lowers R_eq, so R_eq is below the smallest resistance, 10 Ω. (Check: 1/R_eq = 1/10 + 1/20 + 1/30 = 11/60 Ω⁻¹, so R_eq = 5.5 Ω.)

questions.q: A battery has an internal resistance r. Which of the following is its emf ε?
options: The reading of an ideal voltmeter connected by itself across its terminals
The reading of an ideal voltmeter across its terminals while it lights a bulb
The force, in newtons, that the battery exerts on each charge it moves
The total amount of charge that the battery can send around a circuit
optionWhy: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance, so when it alone is connected there is no current in the battery. The terminal potential difference with no current in the battery is the battery's emf.

A student who thinks the emf is the terminal potential difference in any conditions picks this. While a nonideal battery lights a bulb there is a current in it, and its terminal potential difference, ε − Ir, is less than ε.
A student who takes the name 'electromotive force' literally picks this. Emf is a potential difference, measured in volts, not a force.
A student who thinks a battery is a store of charge picks this. The charge carriers are already in the circuit; the emf is a potential difference, in volts, not an amount of charge.
questions.explain: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance, so when it alone is connected there is no current in the battery. The terminal potential difference with no current in the battery is the battery's emf.

questions.q: A nonideal battery is modeled as an ideal battery of emf ε in series with an internal resistance r, and it is connected to an external resistor R that is much larger than r. In the model, charge leaving the ideal battery's positive terminal passes through R and then through r before returning. How does the current in r compare with the current in R?
options: It is greater than in R, since r is the smaller resistance.
It is less than in R, since R has used up part of the current.
It is zero, since r only lowers the battery's terminal ΔV.
It is the same as in R, since r and R are in series.
optionWhy: A student who thinks current divides according to resistance, even in series, picks this. There is no junction between r and R, so there is no choice of path: both carry the same current.
A student who thinks each resistor uses up some current picks this. Charge is not used up in R; all the charge that passes through R returns through r, so the currents are equal.

A student who thinks the internal resistance is not on the path of the current picks this. It lowers the terminal potential difference precisely because the full current passes through it: ΔV_terminal = ε − Ir.
In the model the internal resistance is a resistor in series with the ideal battery and the rest of the circuit. There is one path, so r and R carry the same current, ε/(R + r).
questions.explain: In the model the internal resistance is a resistor in series with the ideal battery and the rest of the circuit. There is one path, so r and R carry the same current, ε/(R + r).

questions.q: In a circuit with a steady current, positive charge passes through a resistor in the direction of the current. Which statement describes what happens?
options: The electric potential energy decreases, and the resistor's internal energy increases.
Some of the charge is used up, and it becomes internal energy of the resistor.
The electric potential energy is unchanged, because the current does not change.
The electric potential energy increases as the charge is pushed through the resistor.
optionWhy: Current in a resistor is directed from higher to lower potential, so charge moving with the current moves to a lower potential and ΔU_E = qΔV is negative. That energy is transferred to the resistor, whose internal energy increases.
A student who thinks current is used up picks this. As much charge leaves the resistor each second as enters it; what the resistor takes is energy, the decrease in electric potential energy.

A student who treats current as if it were energy picks this. The current is the same on both sides, but the potential is lower on the downstream side, so each charge has less electric potential energy there.

A student who thinks charge rises in potential through a resistor, as it does through a battery, picks this. In a resistor the current goes from higher to lower potential, so the electric potential energy decreases.
questions.explain: Current in a resistor is directed from higher to lower potential, so charge moving with the current moves to a lower potential and ΔU_E = qΔV is negative. That energy is transferred to the resistor, whose internal energy increases.

questions.q: An ideal battery and three resistors of different resistances are connected in series in a single loop. Which statement about the potential differences across the three resistors must be true?
options: Each one is equal to the emf of the battery.
The potential differences are all equal.
Their sum is equal to the emf of the battery.
The one nearest the positive terminal is greatest.
optionWhy: A student who thinks every element gets the battery's full potential difference picks this. Around the loop the drops must add up to ε, so three drops of ε each would add up to 3ε.
A student who thinks series elements share the potential difference equally picks this. They carry the same current, but their resistances differ, so ΔV = IR differs.
By the loop rule, the drops across the three resistors add up to the rise across the battery, so their sum is ε. The share each receives, ΔV = IR, depends on its resistance.

A student who thinks the first resistor the current reaches takes the most picks this. Each ΔV = IR depends on the resistance, not the position; the largest resistance has the largest potential difference.
questions.explain: By the loop rule, the drops across the three resistors add up to the rise across the battery, so their sum is ε. The share each receives, ΔV = IR, depends on its resistance.

questions.q: Resistors R₁ and R₂ are connected in series with an ideal battery, and R₂ has the greater resistance. Charge leaving the battery's positive terminal passes through R₁ first and then R₂. How does the electric potential energy converted when one coulomb of charge passes through R₁ compare with that converted when it passes through R₂?
options: It is greater in R₁ than in R₂.
It is less in R₁ than in R₂.
It is the same in R₁ as in R₂.
It is zero in both resistors.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the first resistor takes the largest share picks this. Order does not matter in a series loop: the energy per coulomb in each resistor is ΔV = IR, which depends on its resistance.

The energy converted per coulomb is ΔU_E/q = ΔV. In series both resistors carry the same current, so ΔV = IR is greater across R₂, the larger resistance: each coulomb loses more electric potential energy in R₂.
A student who thinks series resistors share the potential difference equally picks this. The same current passes through both, but ΔV = IR is larger across the larger resistance.

A student who thinks the charges lose no energy because the current is not used up picks this. The current is unchanged, but each coulomb moves to a lower potential in each resistor and loses electric potential energy there.
questions.explain: The energy converted per coulomb is ΔU_E/q = ΔV. In series both resistors carry the same current, so ΔV = IR is greater across R₂, the larger resistance: each coulomb loses more electric potential energy in R₂.

questions.q: In a circuit with steady currents, why must the total current into a junction equal the total current out of it?
options: Energy is conserved, so the energy flowing in equals that flowing out.
The current has the same value in every wire of a circuit.
Current is used up only in resistors, and a junction has no resistance.
Charge is conserved, and none of it builds up at the junction.
optionWhy: A student who ties the junction rule to conservation of energy picks this. The rule is about charge per unit time; conservation of energy leads to the loop rule instead.
A student who thinks current is the same in every wire picks this. At a junction the current divides or combines; only the totals in and out are equal.
A student who thinks current is used up in resistors picks this. Current is not used up anywhere, in resistors or at junctions; the reason for the rule is conservation of charge.

Charge is neither created nor destroyed, and with steady currents it does not build up anywhere. So the charge arriving at a junction each second, the total current in, equals the charge leaving each second, the total current out.
questions.explain: Charge is neither created nor destroyed, and with steady currents it does not build up anywhere. So the charge arriving at a junction each second, the total current in, equals the charge leaving each second, the total current out.

questions.q: The diagram shows four wires meeting at junction J, with the currents in three of the wires and the direction of each current. What is the current I in the fourth wire?
optionWhy: A student who adds all three currents without regard to direction picks this: 2.5 A + 1.5 A + 3.0 A. The 3.0 A current leaves J, so it belongs on the 'out' side with I.
The currents into J are 2.5 A and 1.5 A, a total of 4.0 A. The currents out of J are 3.0 A and I. Charge leaves J at the same rate as it arrives, so 4.0 A = 3.0 A + I and I = 1.0 A.
A student who thinks each wire leaving a junction carries the whole current that arrives picks this. The 4.0 A arriving at J is shared between the two wires leaving it, 3.0 A and I.
A student who thinks the current in the left wire continues straight across J picks this. The layout on the page does not matter; only the totals into and out of J must match.
questions.explain: The currents into J are 2.5 A and 1.5 A, a total of 4.0 A. The currents out of J are 3.0 A and I. Charge leaves J at the same rate as it arrives, so 4.0 A = 3.0 A + I and I = 1.0 A.
questions.working: Into J: 2.5 A + 1.5 A = 4.0 A. Out of J: 3.0 A + I. ΣI_in = ΣI_out gives I = 4.0 A − 3.0 A = 1.0 A.

The wire on the left carries 2.5 A toward J. The wire below carries 1.5 A up toward J. The wire above carries 3.0 A up, away from J. The wire on the right carries an unknown current I to the right, away from J.
